headline: A Graz group shows that the file-change notification interfaces in Linux, Windows, Android and macOS report events on files the watching process is not allowed to read — on Linux that is enough to time your keystrokes.

items.title: Oxygen-vacancy density sorts 50,000 sputtered memristors into seven types
items.dek: Tobias Gergs and seven co-authors at Kiel University and Ruhr University Bochum pooled more than 50,000 current-voltage measurements from 50 wafers of sputtered copper-in-silicon-oxide memristors — resistive switches whose state is a rearrangement of atomic defects — and report that one reconstructed number, the oxygen-vacancy density, organises all seven switching behaviours they see.
items.why_it_matters: A process engineer tuning a resistive memory has knobs — sputter power, oxygen fraction in the feed gas, deposition time — and has had no compact quantity connecting them to whether a finished device switches abruptly like a filament or gradually like an interface. This work supplies one, and says the mapping from recipe to behaviour is probabilistic rather than deterministic, so a fixed recipe buys a distribution of devices instead of a device, and variability becomes something set in the deposition chamber rather than something the circuit trims out later.
items.background_md: A memristor stores information as a resistance rather than as charge, and that resistance is set by where atomic-scale defects sit inside a thin insulating film. In copper-embedded silicon oxide the mobile species are oxygen vacancies — missing oxygen atoms that leave a conducting site behind — together with copper ions drawn out of an embedded metal layer. The same stack can behave two ways: a narrow conducting filament that snaps on abruptly, or a whole electrode barrier that thins gradually. Which one you get has been an empirical property of a particular wafer rather than a designed quantity.
items.deeper_md:
The data set is 50 four-inch wafers accumulated over three years, with SiO_x sputtered at 100–200 W and 5–25% oxygen in the feed gas, a copper interlayer laid down at 40 W for 1.3–1.9 s, a 7 cm target-to-substrate distance, and device areas from 100 to 2500 µm². A self-organising map over the measured I–V curves produces 1,156 cluster neurons that aggregate into seven switching regimes. Inverse modelling then fits a single reconstructed oxygen-vacancy density, in nm⁻³, that tracks both the copper redistribution and the electrical response; the copper–vacancy relation runs from n_Cu,max = 0.50 nm⁻³ to n_VO,min = 0.02 nm⁻³ with 2.53% fit error.

Two caveats the authors state themselves. Their plasma model underestimates the measured SiO_x deposition rate by roughly an order of magnitude, so the fitted densities are effective descriptors and not concentrations. And because the wafers came out of three years of empirical process optimisation rather than a designed experiment, the sampling is non-uniform and had to be reweighted by kernel density estimation. Nobody has published a competing descriptor to argue against it yet; this is one group's reconstruction on one stack.

glossary.definition: A site in an oxide where an oxygen atom is missing, leaving electrons loosely bound; it conducts better than the surrounding oxide and drifts under an applied field, which is what makes the resistance switchable.
The two ways a memristor changes state — a narrow conducting path that forms and ruptures, giving abrupt jumps, or a whole electrode barrier that thins and thickens, giving gradual analogue change.
Defects per cubic nanometre; 0.5 nm⁻³ means about one defect in every two cubic nanometres of film, which is a very heavily defective oxide.
An unsupervised method that lays measurements onto a grid so neighbouring cells hold similar curves, used here to group 50,000 I–V traces without labelling any of them first.

items.fab_angle: MNF's sputterer has exactly the knobs this paper varies — RF power, oxygen fraction in the feed, deposition time — so a club memristor run would be reading out the same axes on the same kind of tool. The usable warning is that two runs at nominally identical settings can land in different switching regimes, so a claim about a recipe needs a population of devices behind it, not one good curve.

sources.title: From Processing to Functionality: Engineering Accessible Material States in Cu-Embedded SiO_x Memristive Devices
On the physical origins of switching diversity in Cu-embedded SiO_x memristive devices

items.title: A junction three orders of magnitude off spec still makes good random bits
items.dek: Y. Q. Chai and three co-authors at Southwest Jiaotong University pulsed a badly out-of-specification aluminium Josephson junction — a superconducting switch whose escape from the zero-voltage state is driven by noise — and got raw bits carrying 0.9981 of a bit of Shannon entropy each, at every temperature from 100 to 700 millikelvin.
items.why_it_matters: An entropy source living on the cold plate of a dilution refrigerator has to come off the same wafer, with the same fabrication spread, as everything else there, and the usual assumption is that a randomness circuit needs a well-controlled device. Biasing at the switching midpoint makes each bit depend on the steepness of the escape-rate curve rather than on the critical current itself, so a junction whose parameters are far from design still delivers nearly a full bit — which means the entropy source does not need a process window of its own.
items.background_md: A Josephson junction is two superconductors separated by a barrier thin enough for pairs of electrons to tunnel through; below a critical current it carries current with no voltage across it, and above that it snaps into a resistive state. The transition is not sharp. The junction's quantum phase sits in a tilted washboard potential, and thermal noise or macroscopic quantum tunnelling can push it out of its well early, so the bias current at which any particular pulse switches is a random variable rather than a fixed number. In qubit control hardware that spread is a nuisance to be calibrated around.
items.deeper_md:
The devices are Al/AlO_x/Al junctions on sapphire, patterned by electron-beam lithography and Dolan-bridge double-angle evaporation, about 1 µm² in area, with the tunnel barrier grown by static oxidation in 1 Pa of O₂ for 30 minutes. The measured junction was deliberately poor: critical current 0.672 mA against a design prediction near 3.09 µA, normal-state resistance 91.5 Ω, and an I_cR_n product of 61.25 mV, about an order of magnitude above what is conventional for this junction type.

Bits come from 0.5 ms square current pulses at 50% duty cycle, with the amplitude trimmed so that P_sw = 1 − exp[−Γ·t_p] sits near 0.5. Raw Shannon entropy is 0.9981 bits and raw min-entropy 0.9271 bits, but first-order autocorrelation is 0.3195 at 1 kHz against 0.0764 at 0.5 kHz — the raw stream is not white at full rate. SHA-256 over 512-bit blocks at 2:1 compression removes that, after which all 15 NIST SP 800-22 tests pass at α = 0.01. The authors call it proof-of-principle: m = 3 sequences of 10⁶ bits rather than the recommended 100, limited by fridge time.

glossary.definition: Two superconductors separated by a barrier thin enough for Cooper pairs to tunnel; it carries current at zero voltage until the bias passes a critical current, then switches to a resistive state.
The worst-case randomness measure — minus the log of the most likely outcome's probability — and the one cryptographic extractors are sized against, always at or below Shannon entropy.
A junction-patterning method in which a suspended resist bridge lets you evaporate metal twice from different angles and oxidise in between, forming the tunnel barrier without breaking vacuum.
Critical current times normal-state resistance, a voltage scale that characterises barrier quality because it is independent of junction area.

items.fab_angle: Worth noting for anyone writing a test plan: whether a device is in spec is a claim about the application, not about the device. A junction that would be scrapped for a qubit passes here, because the circuit needs only the escape-rate curve to have a steep midpoint, and the bias point is found by measurement rather than assumed from the design.

sources.title: A low-temperature entropy source for on-chip true random number generation: universal robustness beyond device quality
SP 800-22 Rev. 1a — A Statistical Test Suite for Random and Pseudorandom Number Generators for Cryptographic Applications

items.title: The bottleneck in word-level PDR is the predicate vocabulary, not the solver
items.dek: Guangyu Hu and five co-authors at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology wired GPT o3 into Pono, an open-source hardware model checker, to propose the predicates, frame clauses and helper assertions its proof search builds invariants from, taking a set of 33 arithmetic properties from 13 solved to 28 within a one-hour timeout.
items.why_it_matters: Property-directed reachability proves a hardware property by inventing an inductive invariant out of atoms it can already write down, so on a multiplier or a divider it fails not because the solver is slow but because no combination of the available atoms can express the fact that needs proving. Supplying the missing algebraic terms from outside therefore changes which properties are provable at all rather than how fast the already-provable ones go, and it turns the atom vocabulary into an explicit, checkable input to verification instead of an accident of how the design was encoded.
items.background_md: Formal verification of a digital block asks whether a property holds in every reachable state, and a block with n flip-flops has up to 2^n of them, so nobody enumerates. Property-directed reachability instead maintains a ladder of over-approximations of the reachable states and strengthens each one with clauses until some rung is inductive — implied by itself one step onward — at which point the property holds for all time. Word-level PDR runs that same loop over bit-vectors and arrays rather than individual bits, which keeps arithmetic structure visible to the solver but leaves open which terms the clauses may be built from.
items.deeper_md:
The implementation is Pono's IC3ng engine with Bitwuzla as the bit-vector solver, and the model emits restricted SMT-LIB2 in three roles: predicates that widen the atom vocabulary available to the minimal-inductive-clause step, clauses injected into the first frame before the main loop runs, and helper assertions that strengthen the target property. Everything generated is checked on the model-checker side — an injected clause must be implied by the initial states and closed under one transition — so a bad suggestion costs time, not soundness.

The headline is the arithmetic set: 13 of 33 for plain Pono, 11 for AVR, 28 with assertion guidance, at a 3,600-second timeout. The rest is honestly mixed. Across 12 HWMCC instances the paper reports heterogeneous results, with one case that plain Pono times out on closing in 3.06 s under predicate guidance; on four high-level-synthesis Kalman filters, clause guidance finishes two cases in about an hour where every baseline hits a 10,800-second limit. The authors state plainly that no single mode dominates.

glossary.definition: A model-checking algorithm that proves a property by incrementally strengthening a ladder of over-approximations of the reachable states until one of them is closed under the transition relation.
A property that holds in the initial states and is preserved by every single step, which is what lets a prover conclude it holds forever without unrolling the design.
A satisfiability solver extended with decision procedures for theories such as fixed-width bit-vectors and arrays; Bitwuzla is the bit-vector solver Pono calls here.
Whether the verifier treats a 32-bit adder as one arithmetic object or as 32 independent Boolean variables — the former keeps structure that the latter destroys.

items.fab_angle: Pono and Bitwuzla are both open source and take BTOR2, which Yosys emits from Verilog, so a club datapath block can be put through word-level PDR without a licence. The paper's arithmetic result is also the warning: a multiplier property that times out is usually missing a term, not missing compute.

sources.title: Enhancing Word-Level Property Directed Reachability with LLM-Driven Semantic Guidance
Pono — an SMT-based model checker (stanford-centaur/pono)
AVR — Abstractly Verifying Reachability, word-level IC3 with syntax-guided abstraction

items.title: Probes inserted before the compiler change the kernel they measure
items.dek: Zhuobin Huang and co-authors at the National University of Singapore and Meta report that existing GPU kernel tracers, which insert their probes before compilation, leave only 8–48% of a kernel's original machine instructions intact, while splicing the same probes into the already-compiled binary keeps 94–98% of them.
items.why_it_matters: A profile is only evidence about the kernel that actually ships if the instrumented binary is that kernel, and a tracer that perturbs register allocation enough to rewrite half the instruction stream is partly measuring its own footprint. Leaving the compiled schedule alone also removes the write-after-read stalls the probes used to introduce, which is why reported overhead falls from tens of percent to a couple — and an instrumentation pass that cheap can run on every experiment rather than on a special profiling build nobody trusts.
items.background_md: A CUDA kernel is compiled twice: once to PTX, a portable virtual instruction set, and again by the driver to SASS, the per-architecture machine code that the hardware actually executes. The second pass is where register allocation, instruction ordering, and the explicit stall and scoreboard control bits are fixed, and those decisions largely set performance — occupancy falls as each thread claims more registers, and latency hiding depends on the schedule. Anything inserted before that pass is subject to being rearranged by it.
items.deeper_md:
The failure mode is concrete. Source-level probes compete with the kernel for registers, and the resulting write-after-read dependencies force waits on global-memory stores that the paper measures at 270–380 ns apiece on Hopper. Xtrace instead runs a backward dataflow analysis over the compiled binary to find registers that are dead at each insertion point, borrows only those, and then jointly chooses the probe's register assignment, its position in the instruction order, and the control bits that resolve hazards. Across three NVIDIA kernels it reports all 53 splices fed from dead registers with no fallback needed.

The numbers: 94–98% binary similarity to the uninstrumented kernel against 8–20% for Neutrino and 13–48% for IKET; runtime overhead 0.9–2.8% against 11.8–75.6% and 3.8–28.4%. Coverage is 19 architectures, sm_70 through sm_120 plus AMD CDNA1–4 and RDNA1–4. The stated limit is register pressure: when dead registers run out the tool raises the register budget or drops from per-thread to per-warp tracing, and the evaluation is on language-model kernels, so the clean 53-splice result is not a general guarantee.

glossary.definition: NVIDIA's per-architecture machine code, produced from PTX by the driver; it is where register allocation and the explicit scheduling control bits live, and it is what the hardware executes.
A register whose current value will never be read again before it is overwritten, so a tool can borrow it without saving and restoring anything first.
A false dependency in which an instruction must not overwrite a register until an earlier one has read it; on a GPU the wait is spelled out in scoreboard bits and can cost hundreds of nanoseconds.
How many warps a streaming multiprocessor can keep resident at once, which drops as each thread's register demand rises — the reason one extra probe register is not free.

items.title: A directory watch reports events on files you are not allowed to read
items.dek: Sudheendra Raghav Neela and six co-authors at Graz University of Technology show that the file-change notification interfaces in Linux, Windows, Android and macOS deliver events for files inside a watched directory even when the watching process has no permission to read those files — enough, on Linux, to recover the timing of your keystrokes.
items.why_it_matters: Access control on these systems is enforced when a file is opened, and the notification path was built to answer a different question — what changed in this directory — so it never inherited the same check; what is left is a metadata channel whose resolution is an event timestamp. Once such a channel exists, anything whose file activity tracks user activity becomes observable, which is why the same primitive yields typing rhythm on one platform and a browsing history on another.
items.background_md: Every desktop operating system offers a way for a program to be told when something in a directory changes instead of polling for it: inotify and fanotify on Linux, FileObserver on Android, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows, FSEvents on macOS. Editors, file managers, search indexers and build watchers all depend on it. The interface registers a watch on a path and then streams back events — created, modified, opened, closed — each delivered when the operation happens. The permission it checks is whether you may watch the directory, which is a different question from whether you may read what is inside it.
items.deeper_md:
The Linux case is the sharp one: a watch on a readable parent directory reports events on child files regardless of those children's own modes, and a watch on /dev/input turns every key event into a timestamped notification, which is an inter-keystroke timing channel — the classic input to typing and password-length inference. On Windows the authors watch the root of the C: drive and receive full paths for files across the system irrespective of permissions, and report a 97.8% F1 score identifying which website a browser is visiting from the storage files it touches. On Android, FileObserver crosses the FUSE boundary that is supposed to keep one app out of another's private media directory. macOS leaks the least.

Linux carries CVE-2025-68788, partially mitigated in 5.10.248, 5.15.198, 6.1.160, 6.6.120, 6.12.65 and 6.18.3. Microsoft added a registry policy, EnforceDirectoryChangeNotificationPermissionCheck, that ships disabled. Android and macOS have no documented fix. The disagreement is over whether these are bugs at all: on the related KDE focus-stealing workaround the vendor's position is that focus prevention was never a security mechanism, and a default-off switch is the same argument in policy form.

glossary.definition: The Linux kernel interface that lets a process register a watch on a file or directory and receive a stream of events describing changes to it, without ever opening the file.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall; 97.8% means the classifier almost never misses a visited site and almost never names one that was not visited.
The Android mechanism that routes each app's access to shared storage through a userspace filesystem layer so that one app cannot enumerate another's private media directory.
Information leaked by how a system behaves — timing, sizes, the order of events — rather than by the data it was asked to return.

items.title: A probe finds the syntax the model's own output head cannot reach
items.dek: Zhenyan Lu, He Wang and Xiaohui Huang put the same 48 sentence-structure questions to seven language models three ways — a linear probe trained on the hidden states, the model's own output projection applied to those same states, and the model's actual answer — and accuracy fell in that order in all 14 model-task conditions they tested.
items.why_it_matters: Behavioural evaluation and representation probing are routinely treated as two readings of one underlying quantity, and this says they are ordered bounds on different things: probe accuracy is a ceiling on what is present, the answer is a floor on what gets used, and the distance between them is a decoding failure rather than missing knowledge. Additive steering along the probe's direction changed nothing behaviourally, which is the part that should worry anyone planning to repair a model by editing the direction a probe found.
items.background_md: A language model's hidden state at each layer is a vector, and two different instruments read it. A linear probe is a classifier trained from outside on frozen states, so it recovers anything linearly present whether or not the model itself uses it. The model's own unembedding matrix — the output projection applied at the last layer, and sometimes applied early as a logit lens — reads that same vector through the fixed map the model actually decodes with. Neither is the same as asking the model a question and grading what it says.
items.deeper_md:
The task is control dependency: which noun in a sentence is the understood subject of an embedded predicate, split into object-control and subject-control items, with 48 hand-curated items per language across English, Chinese and German. The models are Qwen3 0.6B base and instruct plus 14B instruct, Llama-3.2 1B base and instruct, and Gemma-4 E4B base and instruct. The ordering probe ≥ LM-head ≥ behaviour holds everywhere, with no negative surplus in any of the 14 conditions; the widest gap is Qwen3-0.6B Instruct on subject-control question answering, at 0.903 probe accuracy against 0.250 behavioural accuracy.

Activation patching puts the strongest causal layer near the probe-decodable layer in base models and about ten layers later in the instruction-tuned ones, and linear steering along the probe direction produced no behavioural change — so the direction the probe found is not the direction the output head reads from. The authors' own caveats: 48 items is small by design, the mechanistic evidence concentrates in Qwen3, only linear probes were tried, and near-tie items drift numerically across GPU architectures.

glossary.definition: A small classifier trained on a model's frozen internal states to test whether some property is linearly readable there; it reports what is present, not what the model does with it.
Applying the model's own output projection to a hidden state from an intermediate layer, to see what the model would have said if it had stopped there.
The grammatical link that fixes which noun is the unspoken subject of an embedded verb — 'she promised him to leave' and 'she persuaded him to leave' resolve to different people.
Copying a hidden state from one run into the same position in another run, to test whether that state causally carries a behaviour rather than merely correlating with it.

foundations.topic: The Intel 1103 and the birth of DRAM
foundations.subtitle: The part that pushed magnetic cores out of computer memory, and the refresh bill every DRAM has paid since.
foundations.tldr: Dynamic memory stores a bit as charge on a capacitance, which leaks, so the machine has to stop and rewrite everything it is holding on a schedule. Robert Dennard's 1967 patent shows the cell can be one transistor and one capacitor and puts a number on the tax — regeneration every 200 microseconds, costing 10 to 20 percent of the memory's operating time. What actually shipped in 1970 was Intel's 1103, a 1,024-bit part using three transistors per bit, and it did the thing that mattered: it reached a cent per bit, which is where semiconductors stopped being exotic and became the way computer memory is built.

sections.heading: Start with the leak
sections.body_md:
Every scheme for storing a bit has to answer one question: what holds the state when nobody is looking at it? A flip-flop holds it with feedback and burns current doing so, which costs transistors and area. The alternative is to put charge somewhere and come back for it. That is cheap — a capacitance is not a device, it is a consequence of geometry — and it has one problem, which is that the charge leaves. Reverse-biased junctions leak, gate dielectrics leak, and the stored voltage decays toward whatever the substrate is at.

So a dynamic memory is not a memory at all in the sense of a thing that sits still. It is a memory plus a promise that somebody will come round and rewrite every stored bit before it fades. The interesting engineering question is not whether the charge leaks but how expensive the promise is, and that is a number you can actually compute.
sections.deeper_md: The decay is set by the ratio of stored charge to leakage current, and both sides have shrunk with every node. The charge is C·V, so scaling the supply and the cell area together drives it down; the leakage is dominated by junction and subthreshold paths that get worse as the transistor shrinks and much worse as the die gets hot. That is why the retention time of a DRAM cell is not a fixed property of the technology — it is a distribution across billions of cells, with a tail of weak cells that sets the refresh interval for the whole part.

sections.heading: 1967: Dennard puts a number on it
sections.body_md:
Robert Dennard's patent, *Field-Effect Transistor Memory*, filed for IBM on 14 July 1967 and granted 4 June 1968, describes the cell that eventually won: one field-effect transistor and one capacitor. The gate goes to the word line, the source to the bit line, the drain straight to one plate of the capacitor. To write, you turn the transistor on and charge the capacitor. To read, you turn it on again and see whether anything comes out onto the bit line.

The patent is honest about the leak and quantifies it. It states that the charge on the capacitor does leak off, that regeneration is necessary only every 200 microseconds, and that this leaves 10 to 20 percent of operating time spent on refresh. That is the whole bargain written down in one sentence: you give up a fifth of your memory's time and you get a cell small enough to make the trade worth it.
sections.deeper_md: The patent also discloses a variant with two transistors, in which the storage capacitance is the gate-to-substrate capacitance of a second transistor rather than a separate capacitor. That matters historically, because a MOS process of the late 1960s made transistors well and made dedicated capacitors badly. Storing the charge on something the process already knows how to build is a way of getting dynamic storage before the capacitor module exists — and the same instinct reappears every time a new memory technology has to ship on a logic line.

sections.heading: 1970: what actually shipped had three transistors
sections.body_md:
The first commercially successful dynamic RAM was not the one-transistor cell. Intel's 1103, introduced in 1970 on a p-channel silicon-gate process, used a three-transistor cell — and three was the frugal option, because the competing dynamic RAMs of the period used four to six transistors per bit. The cell design came from outside Intel: Bill Regitz's group at Honeywell had worked it out and went looking for someone who could make it, and Joel Karp led the Intel side.

The chip was 1,024 bits. That sounds absurd now and was not absurd then: in 1965 the first commercial semiconductor memory chips held eight to sixteen bits, and by 1968 Fairchild was assembling sixteen chips into 1,024-bit hybrid arrays. A single die holding a kilobit was the step that made a semiconductor main memory a plausible product rather than a demonstration.
sections.deeper_md: Worth tracking how long the better cell took to arrive. Dennard's patent was granted in 1968; the first published design for a 2-kilobit one-device RAM chip came in 1971, and commercial 4-kilobit parts using it did not appear until the mid-1970s. Roughly eight years separate the idea from the product, and the gap is circuit design rather than insight: with one transistor and one capacitor the read shares the stored charge onto the bit line, so the value is gone once you have looked at it and something has to sense a small difference and write it back. Spending extra transistors per bit to postpone that problem was a defensible trade in 1970.

sections.heading: A cent a bit, and the argument ends
sections.body_md:
The 1103 arrived priced at one cent per bit, and that is the fact that did the work. Magnetic core memory was a mature, reliable, well-understood technology with an enormous installed base and a manufacturing process that had been driven down the cost curve for fifteen years; no argument about elegance was going to displace it. A price that could be quoted against cores, from a part you could buy, did.

The adoption was fast. IBM announced its first computer with a monolithic main memory on 23 September 1970. By the end of 1971 the 1103 was the best-selling semiconductor device in the world, and by 1972, fourteen of the eighteen mainframe makers in the United States, Europe and Japan were using it. Three years took computer memory from a woven ferrite assembly to a chip.
sections.deeper_md: Getting there was not smooth. Early 1103 yields were poor and the part did not reach volume until 1971, after several revisions of the production masks. That detail is worth keeping because it is the normal shape of a process ramp rather than an aberration: the first silicon of a genuinely new cell type usually works in the lab and does not yield, and the gap between those two states is measured in mask revisions, not in weeks.

sections.heading: The one-transistor cell wins on the next node
sections.body_md:
Three transistors per bit is cheap compared with six and expensive compared with one, and the arithmetic caught up quickly. Mostek's MK4096, a 4-kilobit part in a 16-pin package, arrived in 1973, the 16-kilobit MK4116 followed in 1976, and Mostek took up the single-transistor cell Dennard had patented at IBM. From then on the DRAM cell is one transistor and one capacitor, and the engineering moves into two places: making the capacitor hold enough charge as its footprint shrinks, and sensing the tiny signal that results.

Both problems got their canonical answers in the 1970s. Hitachi's Hideo Sunami proposed digging the capacitor down into the silicon as a trench; Mitsumasa Koyanagi proposed stacking it above the transistor. Kiyoo Itoh's folded bitline architecture, from 1974, paired the bit lines so that noise picked up on one is picked up on the other and cancels at the sense amplifier.
sections.deeper_md: The folded bitline is the one to understand, because it is a pure noise-engineering result with a hard number attached: it is what let 64-kilobit DRAMs run from a 5 V supply instead of 12 V. The sense amplifier compares a bit line against a reference, so any disturbance common to both cancels. Route the pair adjacent and they see the same coupling from the same neighbours; route them far apart, as the earlier open-bitline arrangement does, and they do not. The cost is array area, because a folded arrangement uses only half the cells on a given word line per access.

sections.heading: What the 1103 left you with
sections.body_md:
Nothing in this story has been undone. The cell is still one transistor and one capacitor. The read is still destructive and still ends with a sense amplifier writing the value back. The charge still leaks, so the controller still steals cycles to walk the rows and rewrite them, and retention still gets worse as the part gets hotter, which is why refresh intervals are specified twice — once for normal temperature and once for the extended range.

What changed is the ratio. Dennard's patent quoted 10 to 20 percent of operating time spent on refresh for a memory whose whole capacity was smaller than a single modern row. That overhead has been driven down by orders of magnitude through bank parallelism, burst transfers and refresh scheduling, but never to zero, and it has been creeping back up as capacities grow faster than retention improves. The refresh bill is the oldest line item in computer memory.
sections.deeper_md: The reason the bill is creeping back is arithmetic. Refresh work scales with the number of rows, while the window in which it must be done is set by the weakest cell's retention, which does not improve with density. Doubling capacity roughly doubles the rows to be refreshed inside the same window, so the fraction of time unavailable for real traffic grows with each generation unless something structural changes. That is the pressure behind per-bank refresh, fine-granularity refresh modes, and the long-running argument about whether the controller should learn which rows are actually weak instead of treating them all as the worst one.

glossary.definition: The periodic read-and-rewrite of every stored bit, required because the charge holding it leaks away; the memory is unavailable for real traffic while it happens.
A read that consumes the stored state — in a one-transistor DRAM cell the charge is shared onto the bit line, so the value must be written back before the row closes.
The differential circuit that resolves the small voltage difference a DRAM cell puts on a bit line into a full logic level, and then drives that level back into the cell it came from.
The two wires crossing at a memory cell: the word line turns on the access transistor for a whole row, and the bit line carries the data in or out of the selected column.
The technology DRAM replaced — an array of small ferrite rings threaded with wires, magnetised one way or the other, read by flipping them and watching for an induced pulse.
An array layout that routes a bit line and its reference side by side so that coupled noise appears on both and cancels at the sense amplifier, at the cost of array area.

foundations.try_this: Open Dennard's patent US 3,387,286 and find the two numbers in the description: how often the stored charge must be regenerated, and what fraction of the memory's operating time that regeneration consumes. Then pull the datasheet for a DDR4 or DDR5 part — Micron publishes its datasheets free — find the refresh interval, the refresh command duration and the number of rows per bank, and compute the same fraction. Bring both numbers to a club meeting and work out where the difference actually came from: the cell, the array organisation, or the scheduling.
